feedback: If a learner rounds 3.47 to a whole using the 7 (→ 4), re-establish the target place and show the single digit to its right is the only decider; have them point to it first.
If a learner rounds up 'because there are digits after', clarify that only that one deciding digit matters, not the presence of further digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciding digit is exactly the one place to the right of the target place (the tenths when rounding to a whole, the hundredths when rounding to 1dp) — never a chain of digits.
learnerActions: Place a number such as 3.47 in a place-value chart and name the place you are rounding to.
Point to the ONE digit immediately to the right of that place as the sole decider before rounding — for rounding to a whole, the tenths digit (4); for rounding to 1dp, the hundredths digit.
Explain why the 7 (hundredths) does NOT decide the nearest whole of 3.47.
activities.title: Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart

feedback: Answer 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole signals double rounding — revisit the one-step number-line comparison.
Answer 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp signals a dropped carry; 12.10 signals a mishandled carry — revisit the 12.9–13.0 line.
Answer 13 (without the .0) signals a lost trailing place — the question asked for 1dp, so write 13.0.
For the estimate, 'exactly equal' is correct here: the +0.17 and −0.17 rounding errors cancel, so accept it rather than requiring above/below.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can round correctly to a stated precision in one step and use rounding to estimate and sense-check a sum.
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (answer 3).

Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole (5 + 2 = 7) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the true total (7.00) — for this pair the rounding errors cancel, so it is exactly equal.
activities.title: Checkable rounding and estimation questions

feedback: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure learner reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder gets 3.5 then 4.
12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: secure → 13.0; dropped carry → 12.9; wrong carry → 12.10.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal' as the correct relationship for 4.83 + 2.17: the rounding errors (+0.17 and −0.17) offset exactly, so the estimate 7 equals the true sum 7.00 — do not require above/below.
Finish by asking the learner to transfer the method to a new two-decimal-place number.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the deciding digit and the carry, in one step from the original, distinguishes secure rounding from double rounding, dropped/mishandled carry, and truncation.
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, then round 3.47 to one decimal place; say which single digit tells you each answer and why not the 7.
Round 12.95 to one decimal place and explain what happens to the whole-number part and why.
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole; then say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the real total.
If you said 3.5 and then 4 for the nearest whole, redo it going straight from 3.47 — which whole is it actually nearer?
activities.title: Diagnostic sequence and probing questions
